nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the historical essay, the autobiography and the literature of the modern
literary_identity: Historian, essayist and memoirist; the author of The Education of Henry Adams and the most searching American writer on the meaning of modernity.
biography: Born in Boston on 16 February 1838, the grandson and great-grandson of presidents; he graduated from Harvard in 1858, served as his father's secretary in the American legation in London during the Civil War, and taught medieval history at Harvard from 1870 to 1877. He wrote the nine-volume History of the United States during the Administrations of Jefferson and Madison (1889-91), the novels Democracy (1880) and Esther (1884), Mont-Saint-Michel and Chartres (1904) and The Education of Henry Adams (1907, printed privately). He died in Washington on 27 March 1918.
literary_profile: Adams wrote the American literature of the modern crisis: The Education of Henry Adams is the great American autobiography and the central American meditation on the difference between the medieval world of unity and the modern world of the dynamo, and its third-person narrative of a failure to be educated invented a new form. His histories are the finest American historical writing of the century, and Mont-Saint-Michel and Chartres is the classic American study of the medieval imagination.
stylistic_characteristics: The third-person autobiography that treats the self as a scientific case; the ironic, epigrammatic sentence; the comparative analysis of epochs through a single symbol (the Virgin, the dynamo); the historical narrative of great scope; the aphorism as argument.
intellectual_concerns: History, progress and the meaning of modernity; the medieval world and the modern; power, technology and the dynamo; American politics and the corruption of democracy; education and the failure of education; science and the second law of thermodynamics.
historical_significance: Adams is the central American intellectual of the Gilded Age and the author of the greatest American autobiography: The Education of Henry Adams is a founding text of modern American thought, his histories remain the standard account of the Jefferson and Madison administrations, and his meditation on the dynamo and the Virgin is the origin of the modern American debate about technology.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Chapters of Erie (with Charles Francis Adams Jr, 1871); Essays in Anglo-Saxon Law (1876); The Life of Albert Gallatin (1879); Democracy: An American Novel (1880); John Randolph (1882); Esther: A Novel (1884, as Frances Snow Compton); History of the United States during the Administrations of Jefferson and Madison (9 vols, 1889-91); Historical Essays (1891); Mont-Saint-Michel and Chartres (1904); The Education of Henry Adams (1907, privately printed; 1918); The Degradation of the Democratic Dogma (1919, posthumous); Letters of Henry Adams (1930-38, posthumous).

birthplace: Yankton Reservation, Dakota Territory, United States
nationality_or_literary_tradition: Yankton Dakota; the Native American autobiography, the short story and the essay of Indian policy
literary_identity: Writer, musician and activist; the first Native American woman to write and publish her own life story, and a leading campaigner for Native American citizenship.
biography: Born Gertrude Simmons on the Yankton Reservation in Dakota Territory on 22 February 1876; she was educated at White's Manual Labor Institute in Indiana and Earlham College, taught at Carlisle Indian School, and published her stories and essays in the Atlantic Monthly and Harper's from 1900. She co-founded the Society of American Indians in 1911, edited American Indian Magazine, and campaigned for the citizenship act of 1924. She died in Washington on 26 January 1938.
literary_profile: Zitkala-Sa wrote the first Native American autobiography by a woman and the founding texts of modern Native American literature: her 'Impressions of an Indian Childhood' and 'The School Days of an Indian Girl' record the trauma of assimilation with a controlled anger that no white writer of the period could match, and Old Indian Legends is the first collection of Dakota stories by a Native author. She was also a formidable political writer, and her essays on the land, citizenship and the Bureau of Indian Affairs shaped federal policy.
stylistic_characteristics: Autobiographical narrative in a clear, restrained first person; the remembered detail of Dakota life; the ironic contrast between Dakota and white values; the spoken cadence of the oral tradition in the legends; the direct political essay.
intellectual_concerns: Assimilation, boarding school and the loss of language; Dakota culture, legend and kinship; land, allotment and the destruction of the reservation; citizenship and the rights of Native people; the memory of childhood and the mother.
historical_significance: Zitkala-Sa is the first Native American woman to publish her own life story and the founder of modern Native American literature: her autobiographical essays are the central Native American texts of the period, Old Indian Legends is the first Native-authored collection of Dakota tales, and her activism made her a leading figure in the struggle for Native American citizenship.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Old Indian Legends (1901); 'Impressions of an Indian Childhood' (Atlantic Monthly, 1900); 'The School Days of an Indian Girl' (Atlantic Monthly, 1900); 'An Indian Teacher among Indians' (Atlantic Monthly, 1900); 'Why I Am a Pagan' (Atlantic Monthly, 1902); American Indian Stories (1921); The Sun Dance Opera (with William F. nationality_or_literary_tradition: Canadian-British; the scientific populariser, the sensation novel and the New Woman fiction
literary_identity: Writer and science populariser; the author of The Woman Who Did, the most scandalous New Woman novel of the 1890s, and one of the busiest men of letters of the age.
biography: Born Charles Grant Blairfindie Allen at Kingston, Ontario, on 24 February 1848, the son of an Irish Protestant minister; he was educated in Canada, France and England, and taught at Brighton College and in Jamaica before turning to writing in 1876. He wrote over thirty books of popular science and evolution, then turned to fiction, and The Woman Who Did (1895) made him notorious. He died at Hindhead, Surrey, on 25 October 1899.
literary_profile: Allen wrote the science of his age for the general reader and then put the same evolutionary arguments into fiction: his 'Hill-Top Novels' and the New Woman stories dramatise the propositions of Darwinism, heredity and free love, and The Woman Who Did was the most radical feminist novel of the decade — its heroine refuses marriage because it degrades women and dies for her principles. His scientific journalism made evolution a common English possession.
stylistic_characteristics: Clear, expository prose; the argument carried by a thesis-plot; the systematic application of evolutionary theory to social questions; the shocking set piece; the plain and deliberate refusal of literary ornament; the travel sketch of Sussex and the Riviera.
intellectual_concerns: Evolution, heredity and the science of society; marriage law and free union; the position of women and the 'woman question'; religion and the secular worldview; the English countryside and its natural history; the ethics of scientific progress.
historical_significance: Allen is the most influential scientific populariser of the late Victorian period and the author of the most radical New Woman novel: The Woman Who Did made him the most discussed novelist of 1895, his science writing reached an enormous public, and he is a central figure in the transmission of Darwinism into English literary culture.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Physiological Aesthetics (1877); The Colour-Sense (1879); Anglo-Saxon Britain (1881); Flowers and Their Pedigrees (1883); Strange Stories (1884); Philistia (1884); Charles Darwin (1885); For Mamie's Sake (1886); The Evolution of the Idea of God (1897); The White Man's Foot (1888); The Devil's Die (1888); The British Barbarians (1895); The Woman Who Did (1895); The Woman Who Wouldn't (1895); The Type-Writer Girl (as Olive Pratt Rayner, 1897); The Evolutionist at Large (1881); Falling in Love (1889); Recalled to Life (1891); Miss Cayley's Adventures (1899); Hilda Wade (1900, posthumous).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the aesthetic essay, the supernatural story and the psychology of art
literary_identity: Essayist, novelist and critic; the pen name of Violet Paget, the most original English writer on aesthetics and the finest woman writer of the supernatural tale after Wharton.
biography: Born Violet Paget at Boulogne-sur-Mer on 14 October 1856 to expatriate English parents; she was educated in France, Germany and Italy, settled at Florence in 1873, and took the name Vernon Lee in 1875. She published Studies of the Eighteenth Century in Italy (1880), Euphorion (1884) and Genius Loci (1899), wrote the supernatural stories of Hauntings (1890), and campaigned as a pacifist. She died at Florence on 13 February 1935.
literary_profile: Vernon Lee invented the modern aesthetic essay: her writing on music, landscape and the visual arts is a psychology of response rather than a history of objects, and her theory of 'empathy' anticipated the whole twentieth-century discussion of aesthetic experience. Her supernatural stories are among the most sophisticated in the language — the ghosts are always psychological and the terror is the terror of a place — and her Italian essays made Tuscany an English literary province.
stylistic_characteristics: Lyrical, analytical prose that moves between description and argument; the second-person address to a place or a work of art; the psychology of the viewer's response; the ghost story that turns on a theory of perception; the essay as a walk.
intellectual_concerns: Aesthetic response and the psychology of art; music and the sister arts; the Italian landscape and the genius of place; the supernatural and the theory of ghosts; pacifism and the ethics of war; the Renaissance and its inheritance.
historical_significance: Vernon Lee is the most original English aesthetic theorist of the period and one of the finest writers of the supernatural story in the language: her theory of empathy shaped modern aesthetics, Hauntings is a permanent collection of ghost stories, and her Italian essays created the English literary image of Tuscany.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Studies of the Eighteenth Century in Italy (1880); Ottilie: An Eighteenth Century Idyl (1883); Euphorion (1884); Baldwin: Being Dialogues on Views and Aspirations (1886); Miss Brown (1884); A Phantom Lover (1886); Hauntings (1890); Althea (1894); Renaissance Fancies and Studies (1895); Genius Loci (1899); The Beautiful (1913); The Handling of Words (1923); The Snake Lady and Other Stories (1954, posthumous).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the novel of heredity, the religious problem novel and the decadent romance
literary_identity: Novelist; the pen name of Mary St Leger Kingsley, the daughter of Charles Kingsley, and one of the boldest English novelists of the 1890s.
biography: Born Mary St Leger Kingsley at Eversley, Hampshire, on 4 June 1852, the daughter of Charles Kingsley; she married William Harrison in 1876 and took the pen name Lucas Malet in 1882. Her best novels — Colonel Enderby's Wife (1885), The Wages of Sin (1891), The History of Sir Richard Calmady (1901) and The Far Horizon (1906) — treat heredity, disability, Catholicism and sexual desire with a frankness that startled her father's admirers. She died at Tenby on 27 October 1931.
literary_profile: Malet wrote the English novel of heredity and physical disaster: The History of Sir Richard Calmady is the story of a man born with deformed legs, and it treats his body, his desires and his fate with a sympathy and a frankness that no English novelist had attempted. Her late novels move from the religious problem to a decadent Catholicism, and she was one of the few women of the 1890s to write about the male body and male desire without apology.
stylistic_characteristics: Rich, elaborate, slightly archaic prose; the family chronicle organised around a physical or moral inheritance; the detailed analysis of religious and erotic experience; the set piece of a death or a conversion; the baroque description of place and interior.
intellectual_concerns: Heredity and the body; disability, difference and the right to love; the conflict of Catholicism and modernity; the burden of a family's past; desire and renunciation; the position of the artist and the aristocrat.
historical_significance: Malet is one of the boldest English novelists of the 1890s and the most important English woman writer on heredity and disability: The History of Sir Richard Calmady is a landmark of Victorian fiction, and her frank treatment of the body and of male desire made her a central figure in the transition from the Victorian to the modern novel.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Mrs Lorimer: A Sketch (1882); Colonel Enderby's Wife (1885); Little Peter: A Christmas Morality (1888); A Counsel of Perfection (1888); The Wages of Sin (1891); The Carissima (1896); The Gateless Barrier (1900); The History of Sir Richard Calmady (1901); The Score (1909); The Far Horizon (1906); Deadham Hard (1919); The Tall Villa (1919); The Private Life of Mr Justice Syme (1923).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the nature essay, the rural chronicle and the autobiographical fantasy
literary_identity: Nature writer, novelist and essayist; the greatest English prose writer on the countryside and the author of After London.
biography: Born John Richard Jefferies at Coate, Wiltshire, on 6 November 1848, the son of a struggling farmer; he became a newspaper reporter at seventeen and sold his first essay to the Pall Mall Gazette in 1877. Tuberculosis drove him to London and then to the Sussex coast, where he wrote the essays collected as The Amateur Poacher (1879), Round About a Great Estate (1880), Nature Near London (1883) and The Life of the Fields (1884), and the novels Bevis (1882) and After London (1885). He died at Goring, Sussex, on 14 August 1887, aged thirty-eight.
literary_profile: Jefferies wrote the English countryside from inside the experience of labour and observation: his essays record the field, the hedge, the poacher and the farm worker with an exactness and a rapture that no other Victorian nature writer matched, and his late work — The Story of My Heart — turns nature writing into a mystical autobiography. After London is the first great English post-apocalyptic novel, and Bevis is the finest English children's book of the rural world.
stylistic_characteristics: Precise, sensuous description of plants, weather and animals; the essay built on observation and memory; the child's outdoor world rendered without sentiment; the visionary rhapsody; the rural dialect and the speech of the labourer.
intellectual_concerns: The English countryside and its seasons; the rural poor and agricultural decline; childhood, freedom and the outdoor world; the mystical apprehension of nature; the collapse of civilisation and the return of the wild; the unity of the self with the natural world.
historical_significance: Jefferies is the greatest English nature writer of the nineteenth century and a major figure in the literature of the rural world: his essays are unmatched in their precision and their passion, After London invented the English post-apocalyptic novel, and The Story of My Heart is one of the central texts of English nature mysticism.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Argentine-British; the nature romance, the travel narrative and the English rural chronicle
literary_identity: Writer and naturalist; the author of Green Mansions and the finest English prose writer on the South American pampas and the English countryside.
biography: Born William Henry Hudson at Quilmes, near Buenos Aires, on 4 August 1841, to American parents of English descent; he grew up on the pampas, collected birds for the Smithsonian, and settled in England in 1874 in poverty and ill health. He published The Purple Land in 1885, The Naturalist in La Plata in 1892, Green Mansions in 1904, and the English country books Far Away and Long Ago (1918) and A Shepherd's Life (1910). He was granted a civil-list pension in 1900 and died in London on 18 August 1922.
literary_profile: Hudson wrote the romance of the natural world: Green Mansions is the great English novel of the tropical forest and its vanishing people, and his South American books are unmatched in their evocation of the pampas and the jungle. In England he became the finest writer of rural memory in the language: Far Away and Long Ago and A Shepherd's Life record a world of shepherds, birds and unmechanised labour with a tenderness and a precision that make them classics of English nature writing.
stylistic_characteristics: Lyrical, unhurried descriptive prose; the remembered landscape rendered with an ornithologist's eye; the romance of the untouched natural world; the plain record of rural labour and speech; the elegy for a vanished England.
intellectual_concerns: Nature and the untouched world; the pampas and the tropical forest; the English countryside and its vanishing rural life; childhood and the natural world; the clash of civilisation and the wild; memory and the lost home.
historical_significance: Hudson is one of the greatest English writers of the natural world and Green Mansions is the central English romance of the tropical forest: his South American books created the English literary image of the pampas, his English rural books are classics of nature writing, and he is the finest prose stylist of the English countryside between Jefferies and Edward Thomas.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the picaresque travel narrative and the literature of the road
literary_identity: Writer, linguist and Bible agent; the author of Lavengro and The Bible in Spain, and the great English writer of the open road.
biography: Born George Henry Borrow at East Dereham, Norfolk, on 5 July 1803, the son of an army recruiting officer; he was articled to a solicitor, learned Welsh and Romany, and in 1833 became an agent of the British and Foreign Bible Society in Russia and Spain. The Bible in Spain (1843) made him famous; Lavengro (1851), The Romany Rye (1857) and Wild Wales (1862) followed. He died at Oulton Broad, Suffolk, on 26 July 1881.
literary_profile: Borrow wrote the English picaresque of the road: his books are not novels and not travel books but a unique mixture of autobiography, philology, adventure and dialogue with the outcast and the wanderer, and their sympathy with the Roma, the Welsh and the Spanish poor gives them a freedom no Victorian writer possessed. His style — plain, digressive, full of extraordinary conversation — made him a model for the English literature of vagabondage.
stylistic_characteristics: Picaresque episodic narrative; long, vivid conversations with strangers and outcasts; the writer's own unapologetic opinions; the documentary record of languages and customs; the digression and the anecdote; the plain, vigorous English sentence.
intellectual_concerns: The open road and the wanderer; Roma life and language; Wales, Spain and Russia; the encounter with the poor and the outcast; philology and the love of languages; freedom and independence of spirit.
historical_significance: Borrow is the great English writer of the open road and the founder of the modern literature of vagabondage: Lavengro and The Bible in Spain are among the most original books of the century, his sympathy with the Roma was unique in Victorian writing, and his influence runs through the English travel book to Borrow's many admirers.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Celebrated Trials (1825); The Zincali: An Account of the Gypsies of Spain (1841); The Bible in Spain (1843); Lavengro: The Scholar, the Gypsy, the Priest (1851); The Romany Rye (1857); Wild Wales: Its People, Language and Scenery (1862); Romano Lavo-Lil (1874); The Turkish Jester (1884, posthumous).
